pages.x: Khufu ruled Egypt around 2589 to 2566 BC. Egyptians believed their king joined the gods when he died, and that his body and his tomb had to last forever. Khufu chose the desert plateau of Giza, west of the Nile, and his vizier Hemiunu, probably his nephew, planned the greatest pyramid of all.

The pyramid holds about 2.3 million blocks of limestone, most weighing over two tonnes, and stood 146 metres high. Its sides face north, south, east and west almost exactly, and its base is level to within a few centimetres. It was the tallest building in the world until the 1300s AD.

Not slaves, as the old story has it. Archaeologists found the workers' town nearby, with bakeries, breweries and the bones of thousands of cattle and sheep they ate. Teams of a few thousand skilled men worked all year, joined by farmers in the flood season, when their fields were under water.

Workers dragged blocks on wooden sledges and poured water on the sand in front, which halves the effort, a trick shown in an Egyptian tomb painting. Ramps of mud brick and rubble rose with the pyramid.
pages.fx: No one knows the ramps' exact shape, but with copper tools, rope and muscle, Egypt moved mountains of stone with a precision builders still admire.

pages.x: In 2013 archaeologists at an ancient harbour on the Red Sea found the oldest written papyri ever discovered: the logbook of Merer, an inspector whose crew of about 40 men ferried limestone down the Nile to Giza for the pyramid. It records their trips, month by month, in the last years of Khufu's reign.

In small rooms above the king's burial chamber, never meant to be seen, the work gangs painted their team names in red, such as "Friends of Khufu". They are among the few marks left by the men who built it.

Two thousand years later the Greeks listed seven wonders of the world. The Great Pyramid was already the oldest of them. The Hanging Gardens, the Colossus and the lighthouse of Alexandria are gone, and it is the only one still standing.

pages.x: The Great Pyramid shows what an early state could do when it organised tens of thousands of people around one goal. It has drawn travellers, scholars and dreamers for 4,500 years, and it is still the one ancient wonder you can visit.
pts: Tallest building on Earth for nearly 4,000 years
Built by organised crews, not slaves
The only ancient wonder still standing
